surprise.title: 57 years ago today, Apollo 12 landed on the Moon after being hit by lightning twice
surprise.body: At 1:54 AM Eastern on November 19, 1969, Pete Conrad and Alan Bean set the lunar module Intrepid down in the Ocean of Storms, within walking distance of Surveyor 3, a robot probe that had landed two years earlier. Getting there was the wild part. Lightning struck their Saturn V 36.5 seconds after liftoff from Florida, knocking all three fuel cells offline, and a second strike at 52 seconds took out the attitude indicator. Mission Control's telemetry turned to garbage until EECOM John Aaron remembered the failure pattern from an old test and made the call that saved the mission: "Try SCE to Aux," an obscure switch that moved the signal electronics to backup power. It is still the textbook example of a troubleshooter recognizing a symptom, which is exactly the A+ way of thinking. Conrad's first words on the surface won a $500 bet with reporter Oriana Fallaci: "Whoopie! Man, that may have been a small one for Neil, but that's a long one for me." On the second moonwalk they walked over to Surveyor 3 and brought pieces of it home. Twenty-four days until you sail on December 13.
